doc.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Orchestration lessons from Tchaikovsky
summary: He learned orchestration from Peter and the Wolf and The Nutcracker scores, and they discuss writing for individuals.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Orchestration is a whole skill in itself, don’t you think?
Yeah. I learned that from “Peter and the Wolf.” The orchestration is bad. The melodies are humorous you know, but the orchestration is bad.
I agree. And like — what’s the Tchaichovsky they always play at Christmastime?
Yeah. That’s with the “Dance of the Sugarplum Ferry.”
“The Nutcracker.” That’s bad. Orchestration is incredible.
So you can learn, you know, you can learn from—
Yes from that man. All you have to do is look at those scores. You can learn everything about orchestration. Because that guy was really rough man. What was going on in his mind, I’m telling you.
Boy what he could have done with the Ellington band.

And you know it’s interesting too because those — I don’t think that guys like Tchaichovsky were actually writing for individuals either. So they didn’t have that extra — like Ellington had such individuals.

Yeah he knew what they could do. But those guys, they wrote for inferior musicians actually. A lot of times the guys that were playing in those ensembles might have been a butcher or, you know, he’s out butchering stuff before he played you know. So they were thinking about — they were able to even think past the fact that they didn’t have all the guys to play the music then like the guys do in classical music now. They wrote it anyway.
